{{Short description|British mathematicians' collective pseudonym}}
'''Blanche Descartes''' was a collaborative [[pseudonym]] used by the [[English people|English]] [[mathematician]]s [[R. Leonard Brooks]], [[Arthur Harold Stone]], [[Cedric Smith (statistician)|Cedric Smith]], and [[W. T. Tutte]]. The four mathematicians met in 1935 as undergraduate students at [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], where they joined the [[Trinity Mathematical Society]] and began meeting together to work on mathematical problems.

==Pseudonym==
The pseudonym originated by combining the initials of the mathematicians' given names (Bill, Leonard, Arthur, and Cedric) to form ''BLAC''. This was extended to ''BLAnChe''. The surname ''Descartes'' was chosen as a play on the common phrase ''[[wikt:carte blanche|carte blanche]]''.<ref name=story>{{cite journal | last = Smith | first = Cedric A. B. |author2=Steve Abbott | title = The Story of Blanche Descartes | journal = The Mathematical Gazette | issn = 0025-5572 |date=March 2003 | volume = 87 | issue = 508 | pages = 23–33 | jstor = 3620560| doi = 10.1017/S0025557200172067 | s2cid = 192758206 }}</ref>

==Publication==
Over 30 works were published under the name, including whimsical poetry and [[mathematical humour]], but some serious mathematical results as well. Many of these publications appeared in ''[[Eureka (University of Cambridge magazine)|Eureka]]'', a mathematical student magazine in Cambridge. Notably, the foursome [[Mathematical proof|proved]] several [[theorem]]s in mathematical [[tessellation]]. In particular, they solved the problem of [[squaring the square]], showing that a square can be divided into smaller squares, no two of which are the same. They also discovered "Blanche's Dissection", a method of dividing a square into rectangles of equal area but different dimensions.<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Blanche's Dissection|urlname=BlanchesDissection}}</ref> They modelled these using abstract [[electrical network]]s, an approach that yielded not only solutions to the original problem, but techniques with wider applications to the field of electrical networks.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.squaring.net/history_theory/brooks_smith_stone_tutte.html | title =Brooks, Smith, Stone and Tutte I | accessdate = 14 April 2010 | work = Squaring.net
}}</ref> They published their results—under their own names—in 1940.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Brooks | first1 = R. L. | last2 = Smith | first2 = C. A. B. | last3 = Stone | first3 = A. H. | last4 = Tutte | first4 = W. T. | title = The Dissection of Rectangles into Squares | journal = [[Duke Mathematical Journal]] | volume = 7 | issue = 1 | year = 1940 | pages = 312–340 | doi=10.1215/s0012-7094-40-00718-9}}</ref> Tutte, who is believed to have contributed the most work under Descartes's name, kept up the pretence for years, refusing to acknowledge even in private that she was fictitious.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Hobbs | first = Arthur M.|authorlink=Arthur Hobbs (mathematician) |author2=James G. Oxley |authorlink2=James Oxley  |date=March 2004 | title = William T. Tutte (1917–2002) | journal = [[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume = 51 | issue = 3 | page = 322 | url = https://www.ams.org/notices/200403/mem-tutte.pdf }}</ref>

"Descartes" also published on [[graph colouring]], and Tutte used the pseudonym to publish the fourth known [[Snark (graph theory)|snark]], now called the [[Descartes snark]].<ref>{{cite journal | last = Descartes | first = Blanche | title = Network-colourings | journal = The Mathematical Gazette | issn = 0025-5572 | volume = 32 | issue = 299 |date=May 1948 | pages = 67–69 | jstor = 3610702| doi = 10.2307/3610702 | s2cid = 250434686 }}</ref> She also published the poem "Hymne to Hymen"<ref>{{cite journal | last = Descartes | first = Blanche |author2=C. A. B. Smith | title = 86.25 Hymne to Hymen | journal = The Mathematical Gazette | issn = 0025-5572 | volume = 86 | issue = 505 |date=March 2002 | pages = 133–136 | doi=10.2307/3621599| jstor = 3621599 | s2cid = 171148710 }}</ref> as a gift to [[H. Pétard|Hector Pétard]] (another fictitious mathematical personage) on the day of his wedding to Betti Bourbaki (daughter of [[Nicolas Bourbaki]], yet another fictitious mathematical personage).<ref name=story />
